sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions

teaching.text: Picture a mass resting on a spring at **equilibrium**, the place where it would stay if left alone. Pull it to one side and the spring stretches, so the spring pulls back toward rest. Push it the other way and the spring compresses, so it pushes back. This pull toward rest is the **restoring force**.
children: The restoring force speeds the mass up as it heads home.
By the time it gets there, the mass is moving fast, and its **inertia** carries it straight through to the other side.

teaching.text: On the far side, the spring is deformed the opposite way, so the force reverses.
children: The mass slows, stops and heads back.
The trip repeats again and again, and that repeated trip is an **oscillation**.

teaching.text: The mass can make this trip in two directions.
children: When it moves along the spring, the motion is **longitudinal**, and the spring itself gets longer and shorter.

When it moves across the spring, the motion is **transverse**. The two spring segments are already stretched tight, and once the mass leaves their line, their tilted pull aims it back toward the line.

teaching.text: In the demonstration, the two directions keep perfect time with each other at **0.5 Hz**, one full cycle every two seconds.
children: They match because the moving mass and the total restoring stiffness are the same.
Nothing in the model drains energy, so there is **no damping**, and the swings never shrink.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate

teaching.text: What makes one oscillator faster than another? Three systems answer the question by changing one thing at a time from a reference that has mass **m**, stiffness **K** and a frequency of **0.5 Hz**.
The first change makes the mass four times larger, to **4m**, and leaves the spring alone.
children: The system slows to **0.25 Hz**, half its original rate.
A heavier mass has more inertia, so the same spring force takes longer to speed it up, slow it down and turn it around.

teaching.text: The second change makes the spring four times stiffer, to **4K**, and leaves the mass alone.
children: The system speeds up to **1 Hz**, twice its original rate.
A stiffer spring pulls back harder at every displacement, so the mass reverses sooner and fits more cycles into each second.

teaching.text: Put together, **mass lowers frequency and stiffness raises it**.
children: Mass describes how much the system resists a change in motion.
Stiffness describes how hard the system is pulled back toward rest.

teaching.text: Rate is judged by counting complete cycles over the same time, and not by how big the swing looks.
children: Swing size is **amplitude**, which is a separate property.

The longitudinal and transverse versions agree in every row because each pair shares the same **effective restoring stiffness**, the restoring action in its own direction of motion. Across the spring, that stiffness comes from tension and geometry, so stiffening a spring along its length does not by itself make it stiffer sideways.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes

teaching.text: Two equal masses sit between two fixed walls, linked by three equal springs. A system like this has **two normal modes**, and in each one every part moves at a single shared frequency in a fixed relationship to the others.
In **Mode 1**, the two masses move together, in the same direction at the same moment.
children: Their spacing hardly changes, so the middle spring is barely stretched.
With the middle spring nearly idle, the restoring force is weaker, and the mode is slower, at **0.4 Hz**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the masses move against each other, closing in and then spreading apart.
children: Now the middle spring is squeezed and stretched hard on every cycle.
That extra pull makes the mode faster, at about **1.73 times** the Mode 1 rate, which is higher but not double.

teaching.text: Both masses take part in both modes.
children: The masses and springs never change, and only the relationship between the masses does, moving together in one mode and opposing each other in the other.

teaching.text: The two patterns can also run at the same time.
children: At each mass, the two motions add, reinforcing where they point the same way and canceling where they point opposite ways. This adding is called **superposition**.
The bottom row of the demonstration is the exact sum of the two modes. It looks irregular, yet it carries both frequencies, and the longitudinal and transverse chains behave the same way.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes

teaching.text: With three equal masses and four equal springs between fixed walls, the chain has **three normal modes**.
In **Mode 1**, all three masses swing the same way.
children: The middle one travels farthest, and the outer two travel less, so moving together does not mean moving the same distance.
No neighbors oppose each other, so the springs work little, and this is the slowest mode, at **0.32 Hz**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, the two outer masses swing in opposite directions, and the middle mass stays perfectly still.
children: The pulls on the middle mass from its two sides are always equal and opposite, so they cancel.
A point that stays still through a whole mode is called a **node**.
This mode runs at about **1.85 times** the lowest rate.

teaching.text: In **Mode 3**, the outer masses swing together while the middle mass swings against them.
children: Every mass now opposes its neighbor, so every spring is stretched hard.
This is the fastest mode, at about **2.41 times** the lowest rate.

teaching.text: The ordering comes from how strongly neighbors oppose one another.
children: More opposition means more stretching, a stronger restoring force and a faster cycle.
The same three masses take part in every mode, with colors tracking each mass and resting marks showing where each displacement is measured from.

teaching.text: These ratios belong to this chain and are not whole numbers.
children: When all three modes run together, they add at each mass.
The middle mass still moves in that mixture, carried by Modes 1 and 3, even though Mode 2 holds it still.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode

teaching.text: The atlas lays out chains of one to six equal masses in rows, with mode numbers in columns. The rule is that each movable mass brings one more **normal mode**, so a chain of N masses has N modes.
children: Shorter chains leave the later columns blank, which gives **21** patterns across the grid.
Every chain has equal masses, one more spring than masses and two fixed ends.

teaching.text: Within each chain, **Mode 1** is always the broadest pattern, with all the masses moving together.
children: Each step up adds another group moving the opposite way.
More reversals create more places where neighbors pull against each other, which stretches the springs more and drives a faster cycle.

teaching.text: The fixed ends stay still in every mode.
children: When a mass stays still within one mode, it is a **node** of that mode, and the rest of the chain keeps moving.
A higher mode is the same set of masses and springs moving in a new arrangement, and the mode number names that arrangement.

teaching.text: Colors mark mode number and rows mark chain size.
children: Every pattern is drawn to the same largest displacement, so a taller picture is not a faster one.
**Amplitude** is how far things move, and frequency is how often they repeat, so the rate must be read from the timing.
Chains of separate masses do not land on the exact whole-number spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics

teaching.text: A **fixed–fixed string** is held still at both ends, so both ends are **nodes** in every mode. The string can only take shapes that fit whole half-waves between those ends.
children: **Mode 1** fits one half-wave, a single broad arch.
Modes 2 through 5 fit two, three, four and five half-waves.

teaching.text: Squeezing more half-waves into the same length shortens the wavelength, and shorter waves at the same speed repeat faster.
children: The modes run at **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz**.
The lowest is the **fundamental**, and the rest are whole-number multiples of it, so they are consecutive **harmonics**, odd and even alike.

teaching.text: All five modes can vibrate on the string at the same time.
children: At each point, their displacements add, reinforcing in some places and canceling in others.

As the faster modes pull ahead, the pattern of agreement shifts, and the overall shape keeps changing. A point can go nearly flat for a moment and then move strongly again, with every mode still present.

teaching.text: The animation is slowed by a factor of **250**, so 100 Hz plays at **0.4 Hz**, and the equal slowdown keeps every relative rate the same.
A **pickup** sits **17%** of the way along the string and records the motion at that spot.
children: Its **spectrum** has one peak for each mode.
The mode strengths were chosen so that the five peaks are equal at this spot. Somewhere else the heights would differ, so equal peaks do not mean equal motion along the whole string.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges. Because a surface spreads in two directions, each mode carries two numbers, one counting the moving regions across each direction.
children: **(1,1)** is the whole surface rising and falling as one region.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split it into two regions, along one direction or the other.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move opposite to each other, with still **node** lines between them.

teaching.text: All five modes can run at once, and they add at every point.
children: Some places reinforce and others cancel, so the combined surface keeps changing shape.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale to fit, so its height does not compare directly with the single panels.

teaching.text: A node is still for the entire cycle.
children: A moving region crosses the flat resting level for a split second on each cycle and keeps going, so that crossing is not a node.

Following one region as it rises, crosses and falls, while its neighbor does the reverse, makes the difference clear. The two numbers describe how the surface divides, not two frequencies or two membranes.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak per mode.
children: The strengths were set to make the peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration** and are not this rectangle’s natural resonances. Their even spacing models how frequencies combine, without claiming that every membrane is harmonic.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction

teaching.text: Science moves forward by stating very clear theories about what the world is like, and in this field those theories are usually **differential equations**.
children: A differential equation spells out how the quantities in a system change.
Solving it produces a **prediction**, a concrete statement about what a real measurement should show.

teaching.text: The theory on the table is that the **vocal folds are a membrane**.
children: When a membrane vibrates, its wave of vibration has **equidistant peaks** in the spectrum, and those evenly spaced peaks are called **harmonics**.
The equations are the same kind already used for springs and membranes, only a little more complicated.

teaching.text: From the theory comes a prediction anyone can check.
children: If a person’s **laryngeal vibration** signal is measured, its spectrum should show **equidistant harmonics**, with equal gaps between the peaks.
The check is an experiment that records real vocal-fold vibration and looks at how its peaks are spaced.
Even spacing would agree with the theory, and uneven spacing would count against it.

teaching.text: What makes the prediction sharp is the spacing.
children: The folds vibrate in any case, so simply seeing vibration proves nothing.

The membrane animation was built with assigned harmonic frequencies, so it pictures the idea without testing it. Only a recording of a real voice can test it, and that experiment is proposed here with its outcome still to come.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end

teaching.text: In a **fixed–free system**, one end is held still and the other is free to move. Each end sets a condition that every shape must meet.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, where nothing moves.
The free end must be an **antinode**, where movement is greatest.

teaching.text: The shapes that meet both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves** into the length.
children: The simplest fits a single quarter-wave, rising from stillness at the fixed end to full swing at the free end.
The next fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
They are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is actually the third harmonic.

teaching.text: An even count of quarter-waves would leave a node at the free end, which the free end forbids.
children: Fitting more quarter-waves into the same length shortens the waves, so each higher mode repeats faster.

teaching.text: The demonstration runs the modes at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed **250** times so they can be seen.
children: They are given equal strengths, so the spectrum at the free end shows four equal peaks.
The antinode does not hold still at its farthest point. It swings through rest to the other side on every cycle, while the fixed end never moves.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free strings were each **tuned separately** to the same 100 Hz fundamental.
children: With the same length and wave speed, freeing one end would cut the fundamental in half.
The matching labels therefore come from separate tuning and do not isolate what the free end does.

lecture12.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization

teaching.text: Springs are not the only things that swing. Any system whose parts keep influencing one another over time is a **dynamic system**, and economists model whole economies this way.
children: **Woodford’s theory** is called **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or **DSGE** for short.
Its name says the economy changes over time, gets knocked about by random shocks and has many linked markets that settle toward balance together.

teaching.text: Picture two lines running across time, one for each economic quantity.
children: The **black curve** follows **unemployment**.
The **gray curve** follows **inflation**.
Early on, both lurch through tall, jagged peaks and deep dips. Once the economy is stabilized, the same lines rise and fall far more gently.

teaching.text: That calming is what **stabilization** means.
children: The economy keeps moving, and unemployment and inflation remain two different things.
What changes is the size of the swings, so that harmful extremes like very high unemployment or runaway inflation are avoided.

teaching.text: The spring and the economy raise one shared question, what drives a fluctuation and what can tame it.
children: In the spring, inertia and the restoring force keep the mass swinging.
In the economy, shocks and the responses of its parts keep the numbers swinging. The calmer curves picture the goal, without testing any particular policy.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency

teaching.text: Everything about these oscillators can be boiled down to seven **principles of mass–spring systems**.
The first two describe the system as a whole.
children: **More mass means lower frequency, and more stiffness means higher frequency.** A heavier load turns around slowly, and a stiffer spring snaps it back quickly.
**A system with n masses has n modes**, and each mode is faster than the one before.

teaching.text: The next three bring in **location**.
children: Added mass lowers a mode’s frequency in proportion to how much that mass actually moves in the mode, which depends on where it sits.
Added stiffness raises a mode’s frequency in proportion to how much that spring stretches or compresses, which also depends on where it sits.

Movement and stretching never peak in the same place. Where the motion is largest, neighbors travel together and nothing stretches, and where the stretching is largest, the point in the middle hardly moves.

teaching.text: That is why one change can matter a lot in one mode and almost nothing in another.
children: A spot that swings widely in a mode is sensitive to added mass.
A spot sitting at a node of that mode barely notices, though it can still move in other modes.

teaching.text: The last two concern the endpoints.
children: A **fixed–fixed system** has harmonics at whole-number multiples of its base frequency, because the base shape fits a whole number of times into each higher mode.
A **fixed–free system** has harmonics at **odd multiples**, because the base shape fits an odd number of times into each higher mode.

The answer depends on what each mode is doing at that spot.

**Mode 5** hardly moves the spot, but its neighbors move differently, so the string there stretches and compresses a lot.

teaching.text: Start with the **extra mass**.

In Mode 5, the spot barely moves, so the added mass goes almost nowhere and the frequency stays put.
Mass lowers frequency only when the mass is moving.

teaching.text: Now the **extra stiffness**.
children: In Mode 5, the string at the spot stretches hard, so a stiffer spring there adds plenty of restoring force and the frequency rises.
In Mode 4, the string at the spot hardly stretches, so the extra stiffness changes little.

teaching.text: Add **both** at once and the two effects split neatly, **Mode 4 goes down and Mode 5 goes up**.
children: The spot is identical in both modes.
What differs is its job, mostly swinging in one mode and mostly stretching in the other, judged across a whole cycle rather than a single frozen moment.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes

teaching.text: The air in your vocal tract can be thought of as a chain of small masses joined by springs.
children: Air in motion has **inertia** and wants to keep moving.
Squeeze it and its pressure rises, so it pushes back, and that is the spring.
Each bit of air moves **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube around its usual place, instead of flowing out of the mouth.

teaching.text: The tube is a **fixed–free** system.
children: At the **glottis**, the fixed end, the air has little room to move.
At the open **lips**, the free end, it moves most easily.

teaching.text: The two slowest patterns of this tube line up with the first two formants.
children: **Mode 1 is F1-like**, the lowest resonance, with all the air moving in one broad pattern.
**Mode 2 is F2-like**, with one more reversal tucked inside the tube.

teaching.text: Three markers show where three vowels narrow the tract.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the model loads the open lips, which are the **free end** of the air column. The air elements there are drawn larger to stand for more **effective mass**, simply more air that has to be shuttled back and forth at that spot.

children: In **Mode 1**, **motion dominates** there.
In **Mode 2**, **motion dominates** there as well.
The free end is where both modes swing the most.

teaching.text: A heavier moving load is slower to speed up and slower to turn around.
children: Wherever motion dominates, that extra load stretches out each cycle.
Both modes slow, so **F1 goes down and F2 goes down** compared with the uniform tube.

teaching.text: The two rows let the same lip spot be compared in two different resonance patterns.
children: Inside the tube the patterns differ, since Mode 2 has an extra reversal.

teaching.text: The shared direction comes from the role the lips play in both modes.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the narrowing sits near the front, about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips. One spot is squeezed, but that spot means something different to each mode.

children: The air there swings strongly in this mode.
Narrowing it adds moving mass, which is harder to turn around.
The cycle slows, so **F1 goes down**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **springiness dominates** at the same spot.
children: The air there is squeezed and stretched hard in this mode, while it travels less.
Narrowing it makes the push-back stronger.
The cycle speeds up, so **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The spot itself never moves to a new place.
children: Its job changes with the mode.
Where neighbors travel together, the moving load is what counts. Where neighbors keep crowding together and pulling apart, the push-back is what counts.

teaching.text: The upshot is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: Adding mass and springiness together does not cancel out.
Each mode answers to whichever effect rules at that spot in its own pattern, so a single narrowing drives the two formants apart.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the narrowing moves back, to about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. Here the two modes swap the roles they had for /i/, while mass and stiffness behave exactly as always.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here is squeezed and stretched hard in this mode.
Narrowing it strengthens the push-back, so the cycle quickens and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here swings widely in this mode.
Narrowing it adds moving mass, so the cycle slows and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: One spot, two jobs.
children: In a squeezing job, the spot itself barely travels while the air on either side crowds in and thins out.
In a swinging job, the spot travels far while the gaps around it hardly change.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 hands the spot a squeezing job and Mode 2 hands it a swinging job.

teaching.text: So /a/ comes out with **higher F1 and lower F2**, the mirror of /i/.
children: Moving a narrowing changes which job each mode gives it, and nothing about mass or stiffness themselves.
The arrows give the predicted direction of each change, not how big it is.

teaching.text: Every spot in a vibrating air column can be described two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**.

Neighbors can travel a long way together with steady gaps, or crowd and spread around a bit of air that barely moves.

teaching.text: The animation pulls one air column apart into its patterns.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights

teaching.text: **Source–filter theory** treats every vowel as two things working together, a **source** at the vocal folds and a **filter** in the vocal tract above them.
Start with the source. The vibrating vocal folds produce a **harmonic comb**.
children: The vibration repeats at a **fundamental frequency**, **F0**, and it also contains harmonics at every whole-number multiple of F0.
In the example, the harmonics are **100 Hz** apart, climbing all the way to **4000 Hz**.
Before the vocal tract does anything, the spectrum is a row of evenly spaced lines, all the same height to keep the picture simple.

teaching.text: Now add the filter. The vocal tract **sculpts the heights** of those lines.
children: Harmonics close to the tract’s resonances, its **formants**, get stronger, and harmonics far from any formant get weaker.
Not one line moves left or right. Only the heights change.
Trace the tops of the lines and you get the **spectral envelope**, and that envelope is the vowel.

teaching.text: For schwa, four resonance regions, **F1 through F4**, shape the comb, with the strongest harmonics gathered at low frequency.
Keep the two axes straight.
children: Frequency runs across, and amplitude runs up, so a taller line is a stronger one, not a higher one.
**F0** is how fast the source repeats, and **F1** is the tract’s lowest resonance, two quite different things.
The vowel is still made of many harmonics. The formants just decide which ones stand out, and these values describe this example rather than every speaker.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the filter keeps **F1 low** and pushes **F2 high**, acting on the very same 100 Hz comb.
children: A strong cluster of harmonics sits down near the low end.
The next strong cluster sits far up the axis, with a quiet gap of weak harmonics in between.
More clusters follow around **F3** and **F4**.

teaching.text: The harmonics themselves have not budged.
children: They keep their even spacing, and only their heights have changed.
That is what lets the filter’s effect be seen apart from the source.

teaching.text: Where does the low-F1, high-F2 pattern come from?
children: The front constriction of /i/ sits at a spot where Mode 1 moves the air a lot, so the added mass pulls F1 down.
At the same spot, Mode 2 squeezes the air a lot, so the added stiffness pushes F2 up.
The two formants end up far apart, the mark of /i/.

teaching.text: Reading the picture means making two separate judgments for each line.
children: How far across it sits tells its **frequency**.
How tall it stands tells its **amplitude**.
A tall line near the low end is still a low-frequency line, even next to a shorter line farther up.

teaching.text: The thin harmonic lines sample the broad formant regions, and the envelope they trace is the vowel. These values describe one schematic /i/, not every speaker.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the filter does the reverse of /i/. **F1 goes up** and **F2 comes down**, so the first two formants crowd close together.
children: In the example, **F1 is at 750 Hz** and **F2 is near 1200 Hz**.
**F3** and **F4** stay higher up.
The source is the same comb as before. Changing nothing but the shape of the tract has turned one vowel into another.

teaching.text: Two different kinds of change can be spotted in the spectrum.
children: When a formant moves, the favored region shifts along the frequency axis.
When a harmonic’s amplitude changes, that line grows taller or shorter.

teaching.text: Here is a subtle point. A formant does not have to sit right on top of a harmonic.
children: The 750 Hz target for F1 falls between the harmonics at **700** and **800 Hz**.
Those two neighbors get stronger because they are close to the resonance.
No new line appears at 750 Hz, because the filter can only strengthen or weaken what the source already supplies.

teaching.text: That is why the two terms need to stay separate.
children: A **formant** is a resonance of the filter, the vocal tract.
A **harmonic** is a frequency component of the source, the vocal folds.
The filter decides how strong each harmonic is, and the harmonics, in turn, reveal where the formants lie.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time

teaching.text: A **spectrum** captures **one instant** of sound. A **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**, so it tracks how the sound changes.
Each spectrum covers one short slice of sound.
children: Frequency runs across it, and amplitude runs up.
The example takes three slices from **/i/** and three from **/a/**.

teaching.text: Turning those spectra into a spectrogram takes two moves.
children: First, each spectrum is stood on its side, so its frequency axis now points upward. A peak on the right of a spectrum becomes a mark near the top of the strip.
The strips are then lined up left to right in time order, so moving right means moving later, not higher.

teaching.text: Second, **height turns into darkness**.
children: **Black means high amplitude, gray means medium and white means low**.
Now height on the page gives frequency, and darkness gives strength.
When a band darkens, it is getting stronger, and when a band climbs, it is moving to a higher frequency.

teaching.text: Watch what happens as **/i/** turns into **/a/**.
children: **F1 rises and F2 falls**, so the two lowest dark bands move toward each other.
The higher bands stay above them and shift less.
The spectrogram lets the changing resonances of the tract be followed through time, which no single spectrum can do.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: Here is a practical puzzle. Formants belong to the filter, but they can only be seen through the source harmonics, since the filter can only reshape frequencies the source supplies. How clearly a formant shows up depends on how tightly the harmonics are packed.
When harmonics are **close together**, formants are easy to read.
children: Take harmonics at **100, 200, 300, 400 Hz** and onward, with **F1 at 300** and **F2 at 2100 Hz**.
Lots of lines fall near each formant, and their heights rise toward its center and fall away on each side, tracing its shape clearly.

teaching.text: When **F0** goes up, the harmonics spread out.
children: Try harmonics at **250, 500, 750** and onward instead.
Now only a few lines fall near each formant, and a formant can slip right between two of them.
One strong line might sit near a formant without marking its center, and it becomes very hard to tell harmonics from formants.

teaching.text: Some voices make this much harder.
children: A **toddler’s** harmonics could sit at **400, 800** and onward.
A **soprano’s** could sit at **800, 1600, 2400** and onward.
Across the three spectra and spectrograms, the crowded rows of lines thin out into a few lonely traces.

teaching.text: Notice what has not changed.
children: The vocal tract can be exactly the same in every case, with the same resonances in the same places.
Only the source is different, and a high-pitched source offers fewer frequencies to reveal the same filter.

Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: A **membrane** is a vibrating surface with fixed edges. Because a surface spreads in two directions, each mode carries two numbers, one counting the moving regions across each direction.
children: **(1,1)** is the whole surface rising and falling as one region.
**(2,1)** and **(1,2)** split it into two regions, along one direction or the other.
**(2,2)** makes four regions, and **(3,1)** makes three along one direction.
Neighboring regions always move opposite to each other, with still **node** lines between them.

teaching.text: All five modes can run at once, and they add at every point.
children: Some places reinforce and others cancel, so the combined surface keeps changing shape.
The combined panel uses a smaller vertical scale to fit, so its height does not compare directly with the single panels.

teaching.text: A node is still for the entire cycle.
children: A moving region crosses the flat resting level for a split second on each cycle and keeps going, so that crossing is not a node.

Following one region as it rises, crosses and falls, while its neighbor does the reverse, makes the difference clear. The two numbers describe how the surface divides, not two frequencies or two membranes.

teaching.text: A **pickup** at one marked point records the motion there, and its **spectrum** has one peak per mode.
children: The strengths were set to make the peaks equal at that point.

The frequencies **100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz** were **assigned for the illustration** and are not this rectangle’s natural resonances. Their even spacing models how frequencies combine, without claiming that every membrane is harmonic.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: In a **fixed–free system**, one end is held still and the other is free to move. Each end sets a condition that every shape must meet.
children: The fixed end must be a **node**, where nothing moves.
The free end must be an **antinode**, where movement is greatest.

teaching.text: The shapes that meet both conditions fit odd numbers of **quarter-waves** into the length.
children: The simplest fits a single quarter-wave, rising from stillness at the fixed end to full swing at the free end.
The next fit three, five and seven quarter-waves.
They are the **first, third, fifth and seventh harmonics**, so the second allowed mode is actually the third harmonic.

teaching.text: An even count of quarter-waves would leave a node at the free end, which the free end forbids.
children: Fitting more quarter-waves into the same length shortens the waves, so each higher mode repeats faster.

teaching.text: The demonstration runs the modes at **100, 300, 500 and 700 Hz**, slowed **250** times so they can be seen.
children: They are given equal strengths, so the spectrum at the free end shows four equal peaks.
The antinode does not hold still at its farthest point. It swings through rest to the other side on every cycle, while the fixed end never moves.

teaching.text: The fixed–fixed and fixed–free strings were each **tuned separately** to the same 100 Hz fundamental.
children: With the same length and wave speed, freeing one end would cut the fundamental in half.
The matching labels therefore come from separate tuning and do not isolate what the free end does.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: Think of a **quarter-wavelength** as the shortest piece of a standing wave that goes from stillness to full swing, from a **node** to an **antinode**. A fixed–free string needs exactly that pair, a node at its fixed bottom and an antinode at its free top.
children: A single quarter-wave fits between the two ends.
That gives the simplest pattern, with nothing still inside the string, and it sets the fundamental.

teaching.text: What comes next?
children: Adding one more quarter-wave would carry the shape back to a node at the top, which a free end cannot have.
Adding **two** brings the top back to an antinode, with one new node and antinode tucked inside.
So the allowed patterns hold **one, three, five and seven quarter-waves**.

teaching.text: Squeezing more pieces into the same length shortens the waves, and shorter waves at the same speed repeat faster. Each allowed pattern is higher than the last.
As the packets appear one at a time, every mode that contains a packet lights it up together.
children: The four modes end up holding **1, 3, 5 and 7** packets, exactly the odd harmonics.
The numbered pieces mark the sections of each standing shape and stay put while the string swings back and forth.

teaching.text: Nobody chose to leave out the even frequencies.
children: Only odd counts can start at a node and finish at an antinode.
The two ends of the string rule the even patterns out on their own.

children: For movement, pick one circle and follow it through a whole cycle.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: Time for a **pop quiz**. Six spots along the air column are labeled **A** through **F**. What is each one doing?

How far its air travels gives its movement.
How the gaps around it change gives its compression.
A single still frame cannot settle the question, since a fast-moving bit of air might be caught just as it passes through rest.

teaching.text: At a spot with strong **movement**, added mass is what matters.
children: More **effective mass** is harder to get moving and harder to stop.
The cycle drags out, and the resonance tends to **fall**.

teaching.text: At a spot with strong **compression change**, added stiffness is what matters.
children: More **stiffness** shoves the air back toward its spacing harder.
When that wins, the cycle quickens, and the resonance tends to **rise**.

teaching.text: **Modes 1, 2 and 3** lay these regions out in different places.
children: The higher modes add extra reversals and so add more alternating regions.
The very same spot can be a swinging spot in one mode and a squeezing spot in another.

teaching.text: So any prediction about a local change needs two answers.
children: Where along the tube is the change?
Which mode is in question? Only together do they say whether a narrowing mostly adds moving mass or mostly adds stiffness for that resonance.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Two everyday dimensions describe vowels, how high the **tongue** sits and how far **front or back** it is. On top of those, every vowel narrows the airway at its own spot. The chart places five words, dean, dune, Dan, Don and done.
Look first at the two high vowels.
children: **Dean** is **high and front**, narrowing about **two-thirds** of the way from the glottis to the lips.
**Dune** is **high and back**, narrowing right at the **lips**.
They share a height, yet they narrow in different places, so their tract shapes differ.

teaching.text: Then the two low vowels.
children: **Dan** is **low and front**, with no numbered narrowing.
**Don** is **low and back**, narrowing about **one-third** of the way from the glottis.

teaching.text: **Done** sits in the **center** with **“No constriction,”** and it serves as the open reference.
Each label tracks something different.
children: High or low is about tongue height.
Front or back is about where the tongue sits along the mouth.
The fraction is about distance along the air path, counted from the glottis.

teaching.text: The narrowing place is what ties the mouth to the sound.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: When the tongue narrows the airway into a **constriction**, two things happen to the air at that spot, and they push frequency in opposite directions.
The air gets **stiffer**.
children: Squeezed air resists being squeezed further.
Where a mode **compresses** the air a lot, that extra stiffness speeds up the return and **raises the frequency**.

teaching.text: The air also gets more **massive**.
children: Bunching air together raises its density.
Where a mode **moves** the air a lot, that extra moving mass is slower to turn around and **lowers the frequency**.

teaching.text: So a constriction adds mass and stiffness at the same time. Do they just cancel?
children: They do not, because the parts of a vibrating medium that **move the most** alternate with the parts that **compress the most**.
Each mode puts those regions in different places, so the same spot can be a moving region for one mode and a squeezing region for another.

teaching.text: The way to see which effect wins is to watch the air through a whole cycle.
children: Follow one bit of air and see how far it travels. That travel carries the mass.
Watch the gaps on either side close and open. That is compression, the source of the push-back.
A tongue-height label or a single frozen frame cannot give both pieces.

teaching.text: One narrowing can therefore work mostly through **mass** for one formant and mostly through **stiffness** for another.
children: One formant drops while the other climbs.
Neither rule flips. Mass still lowers frequency where air moves, and stiffness still raises it where air compresses.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **Mode 1** and **Mode 2** are two ways that one column of air can resonate, held at the glottis and open at the lips.

Mode 2 has an extra reversal inside the tube, so along the rest of the column its movement and compression sit in different places.

teaching.text: Three markers sit at the **back**, the **front** and the **lips**.
children: Each marker is the same spot in both modes.
Narrow the tract at one marker and the change is felt by both modes at once.
The difference lies in what each mode is doing there.

teaching.text: If a mode **swings the air strongly** at that marker, the narrowing’s added mass matters, and the vibration slows.

teaching.text: The two modes keep a tidy ratio only in an ideal tube.
children: With a perfectly uniform shape, Mode 2 runs at **three times** the frequency of Mode 1.
Once the tract changes shape, the formants move and the ratio changes.

teaching.text: Formants and harmonics should never be mixed up.
children: **Formants** are resonances of the tract, and they move when the tract’s shape changes.
**Harmonics** are pieces of the source, spaced by how fast the vocal folds repeat, and they move when the pitch changes.

Narrowing it makes the push-back stronger.
The cycle speeds up, so **F2 goes up**.

teaching.text: The spot itself never moves to a new place.
children: Its job changes with the mode.
Where neighbors travel together, the moving load is what counts. Where neighbors keep crowding together and pulling apart, the push-back is what counts.

teaching.text: The upshot is **lower F1 and higher F2** than the uniform tube.
children: Adding mass and springiness together does not cancel out.
Each mode answers to whichever effect rules at that spot in its own pattern, so a single narrowing drives the two formants apart.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the narrowing moves back, to about **one-third** of the way from the glottis to the lips. Here the two modes swap the roles they had for /i/, while mass and stiffness behave exactly as always.
In **Mode 1**, **springiness dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here is squeezed and stretched hard in this mode.
Narrowing it strengthens the push-back, so the cycle quickens and **F1 goes up**.

teaching.text: In **Mode 2**, **mass motion dominates** at this spot.
children: The air here swings widely in this mode.
Narrowing it adds moving mass, so the cycle slows and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: One spot, two jobs.
children: In a squeezing job, the spot itself barely travels while the air on either side crowds in and thins out.
In a swinging job, the spot travels far while the gaps around it hardly change.
At the one-third point, Mode 1 hands the spot a squeezing job and Mode 2 hands it a swinging job.

teaching.text: So /a/ comes out with **higher F1 and lower F2**, the mirror of /i/.
children: Moving a narrowing changes which job each mode gives it, and nothing about mass or stiffness themselves.
The arrows give the predicted direction of each change, not how big it is.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: Every spot in a vibrating air column can be described two ways, by its **movement** and by its **compression**.
children: **Movement** is how far a bit of air travels.
**Compression** is how the gaps between neighbors change. Tighter gaps mean compression, and looser gaps mean **rarefaction**, air that is thinned out.
Neighbors can travel a long way together with steady gaps, or crowd and spread around a bit of air that barely moves.

teaching.text: The animation pulls one air column apart into its patterns.
children: The moving **Schwa** row is the uniform reference.
The **F1, F2 and F3** rows are the first three resonances of that very same column.
The closed left end holds the air still, the open right end lets it move, and each higher mode packs in more alternating stretches of movement and compression.

teaching.text: Compression and movement are the spring and the mass.
children: Crowded air pushes back toward normal spacing.
Moving air keeps going because of inertia.
Between them, the air keeps oscillating around its usual positions.

teaching.text: Strong movement and strong compression live in different places.
children: Where movement is large, there is a lot of moving mass.
Where spacing changes a lot, there is strong push-back, even though the air in the middle hardly travels.

teaching.text: Watching a single bit of air over a cycle reveals its movement, and watching the gaps beside it reveals compression.
children: Added mass counts where movement is strong.
Added stiffness counts where compression is strong.
Those places shift from mode to mode, and each row is a resonance of the same air, not a separate stream.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The vocal folds make the voiced **source**, and how fast they repeat, their **F0**, decides how far apart the harmonics sit.
The membrane picture comes back first.
children: A **fixed–fixed membrane** with five modes, (1,1) at **100 Hz** up to (3,1) at **500 Hz**, adds up into one motion.
Read at a pickup point, that motion has evenly spaced peaks.
The frequencies were assigned for the illustration, so the picture models harmonic spacing rather than describing every real membrane.

teaching.text: Then come three source spectra, each spanning **0 to 4000 Hz**, before the vocal tract has done anything.
children: At **F0 = 100 Hz**, the lines crowd together, with dozens in the window.
At **F0 = 250 Hz**, from **tighter, lighter vocal folds**, the lines thin out to **250, 500, 750** and onward.
At **F0 = 350 Hz**, from **very tight and light vocal folds**, they thin out further to **350, 700, 1050** and onward.

teaching.text: The pattern is simple. **Lower F0 means denser harmonic sampling, and higher F0 means sparser sampling.**
children: It follows the familiar mass–spring logic.
Heavier, looser folds repeat slowly, and lighter, tighter folds repeat fast.

teaching.text: Any voiced vowel carries **many frequencies** at once.
children: The source decides which harmonics are there to begin with.
The tract then decides which of them come out strong.
So changing pitch changes the spacing, while changing the vowel changes which regions win, two separate jobs inside one sound.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The vocal tract is the **filter**, a **fixed–free** tube with one closed end and one open end, and it picks out **formants**. Its rule fits in two lines.
children: **A formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible.**
**Harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
The source hands over a full set of harmonics, and the filter decides which ones survive. The shape of the vowel is the filter.

teaching.text: Each vowel puts its formants somewhere different.
children: **Schwa** spreads its first two apart, near **500** and **1500 Hz**.
**/u/** pulls both down, to about **300** and **1000 Hz**, with a third near **2000 Hz**.
**/i/ or /ɪ/** keeps F1 low, near **300 Hz**, and lifts F2 far up, near **2200 Hz**.
**/a/** crowds its first two together, at **800** and **900 Hz**.
These numbers belong to this illustration.

teaching.text: Shift the tongue or the lips and the tract’s shape changes, which moves these favored regions around.
children: Each target lifts the harmonics closest to it.
Harmonics in between stay weak, carving valleys between the peaks.

teaching.text: Keep targets and lines apart.
children: A **formant target** is a resonance of the tract.
A **harmonic line** is a piece of the source.
A target can land between two lines and still lift both of them. The filter changes heights without creating new lines.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: Here is a grid that holds one vowel filter steady while the pitch changes. Source rows cross **vowel filter** columns, **dashed red ticks** mark the formant targets, and **colored stems** mark the harmonics after filtering.
Each row keeps one source.
children: The top row uses **heavy, loose** folds with crowded harmonics.
The middle row uses **lighter, tighter** folds at **F0 = 250 Hz**.
The bottom row uses the **lightest, tightest** folds at **F0 = 350 Hz**.

teaching.text: Each column keeps one filter.
children: Go down a column and only the pitch changes, so the ticks stay put while the stems spread apart.
Go across a row and only the vowel changes, so the stems stay put while the ticks move.
The grid pulls apart what the source does from what the tract does.

teaching.text: **Dense harmonics trace the formant shape well.**
children: At a low pitch, lots of stems crowd around each resonance.
Their tops draw a smooth **envelope**, and more harmonics make that envelope easier to read.

teaching.text: **Sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous.**
children: At a high pitch, only a few stems sample each formant.
A tall stem may sit next to a target rather than on it, though the target has not moved an inch.
The two close /a/ targets can melt into what looks like one region.

teaching.text: A formant that is hard to read is still there.
children: The ticks never move down a column.
When the targets hold still and the stems spread out, the source has changed and the filter has not.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: A **spectrum** freezes **one instant**, and a **spectrogram** **stacks many spectra over time**. Two moves turn the first into the second.
Each spectrum covers one short slice of sound, with frequency across and amplitude as height.
children: The sequence takes three slices of **/i/** and then three of **/a/**.

teaching.text: **Move one** stands each spectrum on its side.
children: Frequency now runs up the page, so a high-frequency peak becomes a mark near the top.
The slices line up from left to right in time order.

teaching.text: **Move two** turns **height into darkness**.
children: **Black** means strong, **gray** means medium and **white** means weak.
A band that **climbs** is moving to a higher frequency.
A band that **darkens** is getting stronger right where it is.

teaching.text: Watch out for the horizontal axis.
children: In a spectrum, moving right means a higher frequency.
In a spectrogram, moving right means later in time.

teaching.text: As **/i/** turns into **/a/**, the first strong band **climbs** and the second **drops**, so the two draw together.
children: An upper band dips as well, while a fainter one stays up high.
Joining neighboring slices traces how the tract’s resonances shift, with height on the page giving frequency and darkness giving strength.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: All of this speech science now heads **back to AI**. The plan is a **neural network** trained on students’ own **formants** that decides which vowel is being spoken.
The network gets two numbers, **F1** and **F2**.
children: These are the first two resonance regions that the vocal tract emphasizes.
Two numbers are enough to work with, since the network does not need every point of the waveform.
The tongue and lips push these two formants around in characteristic ways, so the pair carries much of what tells vowels apart.

teaching.text: Input and output are two different kinds of information.
children: The **input** is a pair of measurements of the sound.
The **output** picks which vowel category the sound belongs to.
The measured pair is evidence, and the true label is the answer. Recognition means learning to get from one to the other.

teaching.text: This is where the physics of speech meets machine learning.
children: The mass–spring account explains where F1 and F2 come from.
The network learns how those two numbers line up with vowel categories, using measurements from the class.
For now the inputs and the task are set, and training and testing will reveal how well the network does.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: The vowel network is **purely linear**. Two inputs go in, pass through **hidden layers of 3, 2 and 4 neurons**, and come out as **5 outputs**, one for each word, with **no activation functions** anywhere.
children: The inputs are **F1** and **F2**, always in that order so each position means one formant.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected**.
children: Each receiving neuron is wired to every neuron in the layer before it.
Every wire carries a **weight**, a number that sets how much that incoming value counts.
The receiving neuron multiplies each incoming value by its weight and adds everything up, and that sum is its value.

teaching.text: The hidden layers do the in-between work.
children: They have **three**, then **two**, then **four** neurons.
Each hidden value is a fresh weighted blend of the values before it, not a new formant and not a finished answer.
Because every neuron has its own weights, neurons blend the same inputs in different ways.

teaching.text: The outputs stand for five words, top to bottom **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/** and **/Dan/**.
children: Keeping that order fixed keeps each number tied to its word.

teaching.text: **Purely linear** means each layer just hands its weighted sums to the next.
children: From start to finish, the network is one long chain of weighted sums.
Nothing in that chain turns the five outputs into probabilities by itself.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: One example goes into the network, **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and before any training **every edge gets a random weight**.
The input and the weights do different jobs.
children: The input **measures** the sound.
The weights are the network’s **settings**, deciding how those measurements get combined.
Change the weights and every result inside the network changes, even with the same input.

teaching.text: Each connection has one weight.
children: A neuron multiplies its incoming values by their weights and adds the products.
A neuron in the first hidden layer hears from both F1 and F2, so it holds two weights.
The three neurons there each hold their own pair, so they build three different blends of the same input.

teaching.text: **Before training, every weight is a random number between −1 and 1.**
children: The edges carry numbers such as **0.95**, **−0.91** and **0.28**.

The heading says **blue for positive** and **orange for negative**, though the negative edges come out green in the figure. The written signs are the reliable guide, with the sign giving direction and the size giving strength.
A negative weight flips its input, so some contributions add up and others pull against each other.

teaching.text: These are just **random starting values**, with no knowledge of vowels in them yet.
children: A **forward pass** runs an example through whatever weights are there now.
**Learning** is the separate job of changing those weights so the network gets better.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In the **forward flow**, the input travels through the network **layer by layer**, and what comes out the end is **a distribution over the five words**.
children: In the animation, dots carry the input along the connections from one layer to the next.
At each layer, the values are combined using the current weights and passed on.
That trip is the **forward pass**. Changing the weights is a separate step, the learning.

teaching.text: The illustrated output hands each word a probability.
children: **/done/** gets **0.5**, the largest share.
**/dune/**, **/dean/** and **/Don/** get **0.1** each.
So /done/ is the favored guess, while the others keep a little support.

teaching.text: For a set of numbers to count as probabilities, each must sit between zero and one and all of them must add to one, which these do.
The bars picture the kind of output the network is meant to give.
children: A purely linear network has nothing in it that forces a proper distribution.
So the bars stand for the goal, not a checked result of these exact weights.

teaching.text: One more distinction matters.
children: The **predicted category** is the word the network favors.
The **true category** is the vowel that was actually spoken.
Only the true label can say whether the guess was right, so the tallest bar and the smiley face cannot settle it alone.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: In **PyTorch**, the whole vowel network fits in a handful of lines.
children: **import torch** brings in the library.
**import torch.nn as nn** brings in its neural-network tools under the short name **nn**.
The finished model is stored as **net**.

teaching.text: **nn.Sequential** stacks the layers in the order that information flows through them.
children: A comment in the code marks the shape, purely linear, **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
Each **nn.Linear** layer takes in values and hands out weighted sums.

teaching.text: The four layers match the picture one for one.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False)** turns 2 inputs into 3.
**nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False)** turns 3 into 2.
**nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False)** turns 2 into 4.
**nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False)** turns 4 into the 5 outputs.
Each layer hands out exactly as many values as the next layer takes in, so everything flows through to the five words.

teaching.text: Inside, **nn.Linear(in, out)** keeps an **out × in weight matrix**, one weight for every wire.
children: **bias=False** strips out the extra constant a layer could tack onto each sum.
All the weights stay, learning is still possible, and every layer remains a **pure linear map**.

teaching.text: This code is a **declaration only, with no training**.
children: There are no activation layers, so the whole thing stays linear.
Writing it down neither trains the network nor produces the probability bars. That would take labeled examples and a way to update the weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: Picture the vowel network as a set of columns. On the left are two inputs, **F1** and **F2**. On the right are five outputs, one for each word, **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
children: The inputs hold measurements of the sound, in hertz.
The outputs hold the network’s response to each word.
They look alike as circles, but they do very different jobs.

teaching.text: In between are three **hidden layers**, with **three, two and four** neurons.
children: Reading across, the shape is **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.
Those numbers count neurons in each layer, not recordings or training rounds.
Each hidden neuron collects values from the layer before it and passes its own result along.

teaching.text: Every layer is **fully connected** to the next, so each neuron is wired to every neuron that follows.
children: Each wire has its own **weight**, and all **40** of them are signed numbers, from tiny ones like **+0.005** and **−0.001** near the inputs to larger ones like **+0.6** and **−0.4** farther in.
A positive weight passes its contribution along as it is, while a negative weight flips its sign.

teaching.text: Notice that F1 feeds all three first-layer neurons, and so does F2.
children: Each of those six wires has a different weight.
So each first-layer neuron mixes the same two formants in its own proportions.

teaching.text: The weights stay put in this picture.
children: A different formant value changes what travels along the wires.
A different weight changes how much a wire counts.
Either way, a weight is just one wire’s contribution, never the probability of a word.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** sends the input through the network one layer at a time. The example is **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**.
Start with the top neuron of the first hidden layer.
children: It computes **w₁ times F1 plus w₂ times F2**.
Its weights are **+0.005** and **−0.001**, so F1 adds a small positive amount and F2 adds a larger negative amount.
The total comes to **−0.40**.

teaching.text: That multiply-and-add is called an **inner product**.
children: The other two first-layer neurons do the same thing with their own weights and land on **6.64** and **2.72**.
A negative result is still a perfectly good value for the next layer to use.

teaching.text: Every later layer repeats the same trick on the layer before it.
children: The second layer comes out near **5.50** and **−5.93**.
The third comes out near **1.57, −1.95, −1.95** and **−2.88**.
The layers have to go in order, since each one needs the finished values of the one before.

teaching.text: The five last sums are **logits**, which are scores and not yet probabilities, **0.622, −1.398, −1.300, −0.478** and **−1.076**.
children: **Softmax** turns them into probabilities by raising e to each logit and dividing by the total of all five.
Every probability comes out positive, and together they add to 1.

teaching.text: **Done** wins with about **55.7%**, while **dean** gets only about **8.1%**.
children: Don, Dan and dune land at about 18.5%, 10.2% and 7.4%.
These are just the network’s current guesses, made with linear hidden activations and fixed weights, not the word that was actually spoken.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: Training starts by holding up the network’s answer next to the right answer. That comparison drives **backpropagation**.
children: The **computed output** says **done** at **55.7%** and **dean** at just **8.1%**.
The **desired output** puts a **1** on **dean** and **0** everywhere else, because dean is the word that was spoken.
So the network’s favorite and the right answer disagree.

teaching.text: **Cross-entropy loss** puts a number on how wrong the network is, using the probability it gave the true word.
children: Here the loss is the negative log of the probability of dean.
Push more probability onto dean and the loss drops, and take probability away and the loss climbs.

teaching.text: Then the calculation runs **backward**, from the outputs toward the inputs.
children: First it works out how the final layer of weights contributed.
It uses that to work out hidden layer 3, then hidden layer 2, then hidden layer 1.
At each step, the layer’s weights are replaced with new ones, so **+0.1** becomes **+0.083** and **+0.6** becomes **+0.622**, for instance.

teaching.text: A **gradient** tells how the loss would change if one weight changed a little.
children: The update takes the old weight and subtracts the learning rate, **η**, times the gradient.
A positive gradient pulls the weight down, and a negative one pushes it up.

teaching.text: The activations from the forward pass are frozen while all of this happens.
children: Every gradient uses the original weights, so the updates are really one step taken all at once.
To see the improved predictions, a new forward pass is needed.
The input wires get a much smaller learning rate, because their inputs are raw hertz values, which are large numbers.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: Here is the question. **If we increase this w, will the error go up or down?** The right word is **dean**, but the network is betting on **done**. So the real question is what the change does to dean’s probability.
Take the **pink** connection first. It runs from the top neuron of the last hidden layer straight to **done**.
children: The weight is positive, and the neuron feeding it sits at about **1.57**.
Turn the weight up and done’s score goes up.
Since softmax splits one fixed total among five words, a stronger done means a weaker dean, and the error goes **up**. So this weight should come down.

teaching.text: Now the **blue** connection. It runs from **F1** to the top neuron of the first hidden layer.
children: Turn it up and that neuron’s value goes up, because F1 is positive.
But from there the change ripples through layer after layer of positive and negative wires before reaching all five outputs.
The sign of this one early wire cannot tell, by itself, which way the error will move.

teaching.text: The full backward calculation settles it.
children: For this network and the dean target, the blue wire’s gradient is positive too.
Turning it up would raise the error, so the update turns it down.

Both marked weights end up shrinking. The late one can almost be read off the output, but the early one needed every downstream path added together, and adding those paths up is exactly what backpropagation does.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: Why does training run **backward**? Compare fixing the **last** weights with fixing the **first** weights.
The **last weights, W5**, set the output probabilities directly.
children: The error depends on them very directly.
The gap between what the network said and what it should have said points straight to better W5 values.

teaching.text: The **first weights, W2**, are a much harder case.
children: They shape the first hidden layer, which then passes through two more layers and many other weights before anything reaches the output.
Figuring out how much W2 is to blame for a mistake at the very end is really hard.
On top of that, the effect of W2 on the error **includes** the effect of W5, because W5 sits downstream.

teaching.text: So **W5 is the easy problem**, and the W2 problem has the W5 problem buried inside it.
children: The natural plan is to solve the small problems first and reuse those answers for the bigger ones.
That plan is **dynamic programming**, and **backpropagation is Bellman–Viterbi dynamic programming**.
It works out the effects near the output once, stores them, and hands them back as it moves to each earlier layer, instead of redoing all the downstream work for every early weight.

teaching.text: The punchline is **backpropagation = SGD + dynamic programming**.
children: **SGD**, stochastic gradient descent, is the rule that nudges each weight downhill on the error.
Backpropagation hands SGD the gradients it needs, and dynamic programming is what makes that fast.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To learn, the network needs examples with their answers attached. These live in two **training matrices**.
The first is **Formant_Inputs**, **110 × 2**.
children: Each of its 110 rows holds one recording’s **F1** and **F2** in hertz.
The two columns are the two measurements, and each row is one example.

teaching.text: The second is **TrueVowel_Outputs**, **110 × 5**.
children: Its columns are **done, dune, dean, Don** and **Dan**.
Each row puts a **1** under the right word and a **0** under the other four. That is a **one-hot** target.

teaching.text: A few sample rows make the pairing concrete.
children: **500 and 1500** go with **done**, and **350 and 1000** go with **dune**.
**320 and 2000** go with **dean**, the same example that has been running through the network.
**700 and 1100** go with **Don**, and **800 and 1700** go with **Dan**.
These rows show the layout. The full matrices hold all 110 recordings.

teaching.text: The two matrices have to stay lined up, row for row.
children: The third input row, 320 and 2000, belongs with the third target row, dean.
Shuffle one matrix without the other and the sounds get paired with the wrong answers.
Matching row counts are not enough. The order has to match too.

teaching.text: Keep the network’s guess separate from the target.
children: Before training, the network favors **done**, at 55.7%, for the dean recording.
The target still says dean. Training compares the two and never swaps the right answer for the network’s guess.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: One full training step fits in a short **PyTorch** program, and it uses all 110 recordings at once, a **full-batch** step.
The data come first.
children: **X = torch.load("Formant_Inputs.pt").float()** loads the **110 × 2** formants.
**Y = torch.load("TrueVowel_Outputs.pt").float()** loads the **110 × 5** targets.
**.float()** makes them floating-point numbers. The program expects those files to exist already.

teaching.text: Next comes the network, built with **nn.Sequential**.
children: **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)**, **nn.Linear(2, 4)** and **nn.Linear(4, 5)** give the familiar **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5** shape.
No sigmoid appears between them.

teaching.text: Then five lines do the training step.
children: **sgd = torch.optim.SGD(net.parameters(), lr=0.1)** sets up stochastic gradient descent with a **learning rate of 0.1**.
**sgd.zero_grad()** wipes out any old gradients.
**loss = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(net(X), Y)** runs the network on all of X and scores it against Y, doing the softmax-related work inside the loss, so the last layer just hands over logits.
**loss.backward()** works out every gradient.
**sgd.step()** actually changes the weights.

teaching.text: Each line has its own job.
children: Working out a gradient does not move a weight. Only the step does.
Wiping gradients does not erase anything the network has learned.

teaching.text: All **110 rows** feed this one step, and there is no loop repeating it.
children: The program starts from PyTorch’s own default weights and biases, so it shares the drawing’s layer sizes but not its particular numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: The **sigmoid activation function** is **σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))**. Feed it any inner product z and it hands back a number between 0 and 1.
At the extremes, it pins the answer near a limit.
children: When the inner product is **large and positive**, the sigmoid sits **near 1**.
When it is **large and negative**, the sigmoid is **basically 0**.

teaching.text: Drawn out, the function is an S.
children: Along the bottom runs the **linear activation**, the weighted sum, and up the side runs the **sigmoid activation**.
The S climbs steeply in the middle and goes almost flat at both ends.
Out on the flat parts, even big changes in the input barely move the output. Near the middle, small changes move it a lot.

teaching.text: The formula explains why.
children: A big positive z makes exp(−z) tiny, so the fraction approaches 1.
A big negative z makes exp(−z) enormous, so the fraction shrinks toward 0.

teaching.text: **Lord Edgar Adrian**, winner of the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1932**, gives the biological motivation.
children: **Neurons are nearly digital**, on or off, roughly.
Adrian studied how often nerve fibers fire, so the sigmoid captures a graded response that behaves almost like a switch at its ends.

teaching.text: The same shape shows up in **animal perception**.
children: Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.
Two inputs on opposite sides of the steep middle come out far apart, while two very different inputs out on one flat end come out nearly the same.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: Now sigmoid gets switched on **one neuron at a time**. The input stays **F1 = 320** and **F2 = 2000**, and not a single weight changes.
children: **Purple** neurons are still linear.
**Green** neurons run their inner product through sigmoid.
The nine hidden neurons switch over in layer order, the first three, then the next two, then the last four.

teaching.text: The very first switch moves the top first-layer neuron from **−0.400** to about **0.401**.
children: That one change alters what every neuron in the next layer receives.
So everything downstream is **recalculated**, all the way out to the probabilities.
This builds a real sigmoid network one piece at a time. Slapping sigmoid onto the old stored numbers would not give the same thing.

teaching.text: Once the whole first layer uses sigmoid, its outputs are about **0.401, 0.999** and **0.938**.
children: Feeding those into the second layer and squashing gives about **0.713** and **0.223**.
The third layer finishes near **0.599, 0.609, 0.609** and **0.481**.

teaching.text: The outputs still go through **softmax**.
children: With every hidden neuron on sigmoid, **Dan** takes the lead at about **32.0%**.
**Dean** climbs to about **23.0%**, and **done** falls all the way to about 16.2%.
Same input, same weights, and yet a completely different pattern of guesses.

teaching.text: None of this is training.
children: Dean’s share rose from 8.1%, but Dan still beats it.
So changing the activation rule can change which word the network favors without the network having learned the right answer.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The PyTorch program for the sigmoid network is the earlier program with sigmoid slipped in after each hidden layer.
children: It still loads **X**, the **110 × 2** formants, and **Y**, the **110 × 5** targets.
**nn.Sigmoid()** now follows **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)** and **nn.Linear(2, 4)**.
Each hidden layer adds up its inputs and then squashes the sums before passing them on.

teaching.text: Sigmoid reshapes values but never changes how many there are.
children: Three values going in are three values coming out, so **nn.Linear(3, 2)** still gets exactly the size it expects.
The same goes for the two-value and four-value layers, so the shape stays **2 to 3 to 2 to 4 to 5**.

teaching.text: The last layer, **nn.Linear(4, 5)**, gets no sigmoid.
children: Its five logits go straight to **CrossEntropyLoss**, which does the softmax-related work itself.
The hidden sigmoids and the final word probabilities have separate jobs, and no hidden neuron turns into one of the five words.

teaching.text: The training lines do not change at all.
children: **zero_grad**, the forward pass and its loss, **backward**, then **step**.
The learning rate is still **0.1**, and all 110 recordings feed the one step.

teaching.text: The drawing and the code start from different places.
children: The drawing uses the original illustrative weights with no biases, which is how Dan gets **32.0%** and dean **23.0%**.
The code starts from PyTorch’s defaults, so it copies the structure, and only the same starting weights and bias choices would copy those exact numbers.
